negligible

NEG-lih-juh-bul -- shares a root with 'eligible,' both from a Latin word meaning to choose or gather. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Negligible is so small or unimportant that it is not worth considering.

The difference in price between the two brands was negligible, just a few cents.

Worked Example

A scientist measures the tiny amount of heat lost by a well-insulated thermos over an entire day and finds the change so small it barely registers on even the most sensitive thermometer.

That amount so small it's essentially not worth worrying about is exactly what negligible describes. Unlike 'significant,' which demands attention, negligible can safely be set aside.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

trivial: Trivial dismisses something as too minor to deserve attention -- a trivial detail, a trivial complaint. Negligible is more measured and often numerical: an amount or effect so small it can safely be ignored. Trivial mocks a thing's importance; negligible reports its size.

paltry: Paltry belittles an amount as ridiculously small and inadequate -- a paltry raise insults the person who receives it. Negligible passes no such judgment: it simply means the amount is too small to be worth considering. A negligible fee is ignorable; a paltry fee is embarrassing.

slight: Slight means small in size or degree -- a slight delay, a slight breeze -- and it says nothing about whether the thing matters. Negligible makes that further claim: the amount is so small it can safely be set aside. A slight change might still be important; a negligible one never is.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

substantial: of considerable importance, size, or worth

significant: sufficiently great to be worthy of attention

Where it sits · how safely it can be ignored — minimal → negligible → insignificant

minimal vs. negligible: Minimal is a bit more neutral than negligible -- minimal simply describes the smallest possible amount, while negligible specifically implies the amount is so small it can be safely disregarded.

insignificant vs. negligible: Insignificant can feel like a stronger dismissal than negligible: negligible often applies to a measurable quantity being very small, while insignificant more broadly dismisses something's importance or relevance altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — neg-

Prefix — neg-: not (Latin)

Root — lig

Root — lig: to choose, gather (from Latin legere, as in negligere, 'to disregard')

Suffix — -ible

Suffix — -ible: able to be (Latin -ibilis)

Put it together

Put it together: Neg- ('not') + lig ('to choose, gather' — from Latin legere) + -ible ('able to be'): Latin negligere meant 'to disregard' or 'neglect.' Something negligible, at its root, is not worth choosing to notice — so small it can be set aside without consequence, sharing its root with eligible.

Use the root in a new word: eligible

Use the root in a new word: eligible: Only students with a 3.0 average or higher were eligible to apply for the scholarship.
